title: The Book of Proverbs Timeline
sub: Wisdom's Public Call · Two Roads, Two Houses, Two Women
desc: Nine chapters of sustained fatherly discourse on acquiring wisdom and avoiding the adulterous woman give way to hundreds of two-line sayings on wealth, speech, kings, and the fear of the LORD, closing on an acrostic portrait of the wife whose worth is 'far more than rubies.'

eras.label: Era One · Proverbs 1
eras.name: The Purpose of the Proverbs, and Wisdom's Public Appeal
eras.dates: Solomon states his purpose outright, to teach skillful living and the fear of the LORD, then a father warns his son against violent men before Wisdom herself, personified as a woman, cries out in the streets and warns that those who refuse her now will call for her too late.

events.title: The Purpose of the Proverbs
events.detail: The book opens by naming its own goal (wisdom, discipline, discernment, and skillful living for the naive and the wise alike) and states its governing thesis in a single line that will recur throughout: reverence for God is where real knowledge begins.

verses.text: Fearing the LORD [Yahweh] is the beginning of discernment, but fools have despised wisdom and moral instruction.

events.title: A Father's Warning Against Violent Men
events.detail: A father warns his son not to join sinners who entice with promises of easy plunder gained by ambush and bloodshed, closing with the book's recurring irony: those who set traps for others are really setting traps for their own lives.

verses.text: But these men lie in wait for their own blood; they ambush their own lives! Such are the ways of all who gain profit unjustly; it takes away the life of those who obtain it!

events.title: Wisdom Cries Out in the Streets
events.detail: Wisdom is personified as a woman shouting in the city squares, pleading with the naive to listen while there is time, and warning that those who mock her now will one day call out to her in disaster and find she will not answer.

verses.text: Because I called but you refused to listen… I myself will laugh when disaster strikes you; I will mock when what you dread comes.

eras.label: Era Two · Proverbs 2
eras.name: The Rewards of Seeking Wisdom Like Hidden Treasure
eras.dates: A single long sentence stretching across the whole chapter promises that wisdom, sought as urgently as silver, will guard its seeker from two dangers in particular: men who walk crooked paths and the seductive words of the adulterous woman.

events.title: Seek Wisdom Like Silver
events.detail: The father urges his son to search for wisdom with the same urgency as buried treasure, promising that the LORD himself is the source who grants it, and that discretion and understanding will stand guard over the one who finds it.

verses.text: then you will understand how to fear the LORD [Yahweh], and you will discover knowledge about God [Elohim]. For the LORD [Yahweh] gives wisdom, and from his mouth comes knowledge and understanding.

events.title: Delivered From Crooked Men and the Adulterous Woman
events.detail: Wisdom is framed as protection from two dangers named together for the first time: men who delight in perverse evil, and "the loose woman who has flattered you with her words," whose house is said to lead down to death itself.

verses.text: to deliver you from the adulterous woman, from the loose woman who has flattered you with her words, who leaves the husband from her younger days and has ignored her marriage covenant made before God [Elohim].

eras.label: Era Three · Proverbs 3
eras.name: Trust in the LORD, and the Surpassing Value of Wisdom
eras.dates: One of the most quoted chapters in the book: trust the LORD rather than your own understanding, honor him with the first of your wealth, and prize wisdom above silver, gold, and rubies, because it was wisdom by which he laid the earth's own foundations.

events.title: "Trust in the LORD With All Your Heart"
events.detail: The chapter's opening command becomes the book's most familiar line, trust the LORD rather than lean on your own understanding, followed by instruction to honor him with the firstfruits of wealth and not resent his discipline, since it is proof of a father's love.

verses.text: Trust in the LORD [Yahweh] with all your heart, and do not rely on your own understanding. Acknowledge him in all your ways, and he will make your paths straight.

events.title: Wisdom More Precious Than Rubies
events.detail: Wisdom is praised as more valuable than silver, gold, or rubies, holding long life in one hand and riches in the other, and the chapter grounds that value cosmically, stating that it was by wisdom that the LORD founded the earth and set the heavens in place.

verses.text: By wisdom the LORD [Yahweh] laid the foundation of the earth; he established the heavens by understanding. By his knowledge the primordial sea was broken open, so that the clouds drip down dew.

events.title: Practical Ethics With a Neighbor
events.detail: The discourse turns concrete (do not withhold help you are able to give, do not plot against a trusting neighbor, do not envy a violent man) closing on the principle that the LORD opposes the proud but gives favor to the humble.

verses.text: The LORD's [Yahweh's] curse is on the household of the wicked, but he blesses the home of the righteous. With arrogant scoffers he is scornful, yet he shows favor to the humble.

eras.label: Era Four · Proverbs 4
eras.name: A Father's Charge: "Acquire Wisdom, Acquire Understanding"
eras.dates: Solomon recalls being taught the same lesson by his own father David, then sets before his son the book's central image of two roads: the bright path of the righteous that grows steadily brighter, and the way of the wicked, who stumble in darkness without knowing what trips them.

events.title: Solomon Recalls His Own Father's Instruction
events.detail: Solomon reaches back a generation, recalling how his own father taught him to "acquire wisdom, acquire understanding" above everything else, grounding the book's advice in a real, remembered family transmission rather than abstract theory.

events.title: Two Paths: Light and Darkness
events.detail: The chapter's central image contrasts the path of the righteous, "like the bright morning light, growing brighter and brighter until full day," with the way of the wicked, who stumble in gloom without even knowing what makes them fall.

verses.text: But the path of the righteous is like the bright morning light, growing brighter and brighter until full day. The way of the wicked is like gloomy darkness; they do not know what they stumble over.

events.title: Guard Your Heart
events.detail: The chapter closes with instruction to guard the heart above everything else, since it is the source from which all of life flows, and to keep the eyes fixed straight ahead rather than turning to the right or the left.

verses.text: Guard your heart with all vigilance, for from it are the sources of life.

eras.label: Era Five · Proverbs 5
eras.name: Warning Against the Adulterous Woman, and Joy in the Wife of Youth
eras.dates: The first of the book's extended warnings against sexual sin: her words drip honey but end bitter as wormwood, and a man who follows her forfeits his strength, his years, and his reputation, so the chapter turns instead to rejoicing in the wife of one's own youth.

events.title: Her Lips Drip Honey, but Her End Is Bitter
events.detail: The adulterous woman's seductive speech is described as honey and smooth oil at first, but her final end is as bitter as wormwood and sharp as a sword, and the son is warned he could lose his strength, his years, and his standing "in the midst of the whole congregation" to her.

verses.text: For the lips of the adulterous woman drip honey, and her seductive words are smoother than olive oil, but in the end she is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a two-edged sword.

events.title: "Drink From Your Own Cistern": Joy in the Wife of Youth
events.detail: The positive counterpart to the warning: drink water from your own well rather than a stranger's, and rejoice in "the wife you married in your youth", closing with the sobering reminder that the LORD sees every path a person walks.

verses.text: May your fountain be blessed, and may you rejoice in the wife you married in your youth.

eras.label: Era Six · Proverbs 6
eras.name: Four Warnings: Surety, Sloth, Wickedness, and Adultery
eras.dates: A chapter of loosely joined but memorable warnings: against co-signing a stranger's debt, against the sluggard who could learn from the ant, against seven things the LORD hates by name, and a return to the danger of adultery, this time stated in blunter economic and physical terms.

events.title: Warning Against Putting Up Security
events.detail: A short, urgent warning against becoming a guarantor for a stranger's debt, telling the son to free himself "like a gazelle from a snare" before the obligation traps him.

events.title: "Go to the Ant, You Sluggard"
events.detail: One of the book's most familiar images: the sluggard is sent to study the ant, which stores up food in summer with no commander or overseer to force it, so that poverty does not arrive on the sluggard "like a robber."

verses.text: Go to the ant, you sluggard; observe her ways and be wise!

events.title: The Seven Things the LORD Hates
events.detail: A rare numbered list names seven specific things the LORD hates by name: haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood, a heart devising wicked plans, feet swift to run to evil, a false witness, and one who spreads discord among family.

verses.text: There are six things that the LORD [Yahweh] hates, even seven things that are an abomination to him: haughty eyes, a lying tongue, and hands that shed innocent blood.

events.title: Adultery Restated in Blunter Terms
events.detail: The warning against the adulterous woman returns in starker imagery: a man who sleeps with his neighbor's wife is compared to someone who carries fire against his own chest and expects not to be burned, facing a jealous husband who "will not show mercy when he takes revenge."

verses.text: Can a man hold fire against his chest without burning his clothes?… So it is with the one who sleeps with his neighbor's wife; no one who touches her will escape punishment.

eras.label: Era Seven · Proverbs 7
eras.name: The Seduction of the Naive Young Man
eras.dates: The book's single most extended narrative scene: a father recalls watching from his window as a "young man who lacked sense" is met, flattered, and led step by step into a stranger's bed, likened to an ox walking unknowingly to slaughter.

events.title: "Bind Them on Your Forearm"
events.detail: The father again urges his son to treat wisdom as intimately as family, calling her "my sister," so that she will keep him from the very scene the chapter is about to narrate.

events.title: A Young Man Led to Slaughter Like an Ox
events.detail: In a vivid first-person narrative, the father recalls watching from his window as an inexperienced young man is met at twilight by a woman "dressed like a prostitute," flattered with promises of secret pleasure, and led away "like an ox that goes to the slaughter": the chapter's most cinematic scene in the whole book.

verses.text: She turned him aside with her persuasions; with her smooth talk she was enticing him along. Suddenly he was going after her like an ox that goes to the slaughter… he does not know that it will cost him his life.

events.title: "Her House Is the Way to the Grave"
events.detail: The narrative closes with a direct application to the listening son: her house is the road to death, and "all those she has slain are many": the strongest statement yet of what is actually at stake in these repeated warnings.

verses.text: Her house is the way to the grave, going down to the chambers of death.

eras.label: Era Eight · Proverbs 8
eras.name: Wisdom's Own Speech: Her Value, and Her Role in Creation
eras.dates: For the only time in the book, Wisdom speaks in her own extended first-person voice: publicly inviting all people to hear her, claiming she was present with God before the mountains or the sea existed, working beside him as creation's own master craftsman.

events.title: Wisdom's Public Call
events.detail: Wisdom again calls out publicly, this time cataloguing her own worth directly: better than rubies, and incomparable to anything else people might desire.

verses.text: For wisdom is better than rubies, and desirable things cannot be compared to her.

events.title: Wisdom and the Reign of Kings
events.detail: Wisdom claims that it is by her that "kings reign" and rulers decree justice, and that those who love her inherit real, lasting wealth rather than fleeting riches.

verses.text: By me, kings reign, and by me, potentates decree righteousness; by me, princes rule, as well as nobles and all righteous judges.

events.title: Wisdom Present at Creation
events.detail: In the chapter's climactic and most theologically weighted passage, Wisdom describes being brought forth by the LORD before the mountains, the springs, or the sea existed, standing beside him "as a master craftsman" and rejoicing in the world as it was being made.

verses.text: The LORD [Yahweh] created me as the beginning of his works, before his deeds of long ago. From eternity I have been fashioned, from the beginning, from before the world existed.

events.title: "Blessed Is the One Who Listens to Me"
events.detail: Wisdom closes her speech with a direct blessing on those who wait at her doors daily, and a stark warning that whoever misses her "loves death."

verses.text: For the one who finds me has found life and received favor from the LORD [Yahweh]. But the one who misses me brings harm to himself; all who hate me love death.

eras.label: Era Nine · Proverbs 9
eras.name: Two Houses, Two Invitations: Wisdom and Folly
eras.dates: The nine-chapter prologue closes with a deliberate contrast staged as two competing dinner invitations: Wisdom, who has built a seven-pillared house and prepared a real meal, against Folly, a loud and undisciplined woman offering only stolen water that ends in the grave.

events.title: Wisdom's House and Her Invitation
events.detail: Wisdom is pictured as a host who has built her own house on seven pillars, prepared meat and wine, and sent servants out to invite the naive in to eat and "proceed in the way of understanding."

verses.text: Wisdom has built her house; she has carved out its seven pillars. She has prepared her meat, she has mixed her wine; she also has arranged her table.

events.title: On Correcting Mockers Versus the Wise
events.detail: A short aside on the difference between correcting a mocker, who will only hate the one who reproves him, and correcting a wise person, who will love his corrector and grow wiser still, grounding it once more in the fear of the LORD.

verses.text: The beginning of wisdom is to fear the LORD [Yahweh], and acknowledging the Holy One is understanding.

events.title: Folly's House and Her Invitation
events.detail: The deliberate counterpart to Wisdom's banquet: Folly sits at her own door offering "stolen waters" that are sweet in the moment, but her unsuspecting guests do not realize "that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of the grave."

verses.text: "Stolen waters are sweet, and food obtained in secret is pleasant!" But they do not realize that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of the grave.

eras.label: Era Ten · Proverbs 10-11
eras.name: Solomon's Proverbs Begin: Wealth, Integrity, and the Tongue
eras.dates: "The proverbs of Solomon" formally begins at 10:1, launching several hundred largely self-contained two-line sayings built on antithetic parallelism (the righteous against the wicked, the wise against the fool) with these opening chapters weighted toward wealth honestly gained, careful speech, and the trustworthiness of a person's character.

events.title: Chapter 10: Wise Sons, Diligent Hands, and Guarded Speech
events.detail: A dense chapter of one-line contrasts sets the pattern for the rest of the book: a wise son versus a foolish one, diligence versus laziness, and repeated attention to speech: "the one who restrains his words is wise," while a talkative fool comes to ruin.

verses.text: When words abound, transgression is inevitable, but the one who restrains his words is wise.
The blessing from the LORD [Yahweh] makes a person rich, and he adds no sorrow to it.

events.title: Chapter 11: Honest Scales, Community, and Generosity
events.detail: The chapter opens with the LORD's own abhorrence of dishonest scales and closes on generosity: the one who is generous is enriched further, while withholding more than one should leads only to poverty, and a whole city is said to rise or fall by the character of its people.

verses.text: The LORD [Yahweh] abhors dishonest scales, but an accurate weight is his delight.
One person is generous and yet grows more wealthy, but another withholds more than he should and comes to poverty. A generous person will be enriched.

eras.label: Era Eleven · Proverbs 12-13
eras.name: Discipline, Speech, and the Household
eras.dates: These chapters return often to the tongue (the words of the wise bring healing, and a faithful witness tells the truth) while also weighing a wise son's response to discipline against a scoffer who has never once listened to correction.

events.title: Chapter 12: Loving Discipline, Truthful Speech
events.detail: Loving discipline is equated with loving knowledge itself, and honest speech is praised repeatedly: "the faithful witness tells what is right," while reckless words are compared to "the thrusts of a sword."

verses.text: Speaking recklessly is like the thrusts of a sword, but the words of the wise bring healing.

events.title: Chapter 13: A Wise Son Accepts Discipline
events.detail: The chapter opens by naming its own theme directly (a wise son accepts his father's discipline, but a scoffer has never listened to rebuke) and closes with the well-known instruction that sparing the rod is, in effect, a failure to truly love a child.

verses.text: A wise son accepts his father's discipline, but a scoffer has never listened to rebuke.
The one who spares his rod hates his child, but the one who loves his child is diligent in disciplining him.

eras.label: Era Twelve · Proverbs 14-15
eras.name: Wisdom in the Home, and the Fear of the LORD
eras.dates: Two chapters saturated with direct statements about the LORD: his eyes watch every place, he abhors the sacrifice of the wicked yet delights in the prayer of the upright, and "in the fear of the LORD one has strong confidence," a refuge extending even to one's own children.

events.title: Chapter 14: A Wise Woman Builds Her House
events.detail: The chapter opens by crediting a household's stability or ruin to its women, then moves through a wide range of sayings on truth, temper, and the oppression of the poor, closing with the claim that "righteousness exalts a nation, but sin is a disgrace to any people."

verses.text: Every wise woman has built her household, but a foolish woman tears it down with her own hands.
The one who oppresses the poor has insulted his Creator, but whoever honors him shows favor to the needy.

events.title: Chapter 15: "The Eyes of the LORD Are in Every Place"
events.detail: One of the book's most concentrated runs of direct statements about God: his eyes watch every place, he abhors the sacrifice of the wicked but loves the prayer of the upright, and the fear of the LORD is called both a life-giving fountain and "before honor comes humility."

verses.text: The eyes of the LORD [Yahweh] are in every place, keeping watch on those who are evil and those who are good.
The LORD [Yahweh] abhors the sacrifice of the wicked, but the prayer of the upright pleases him.

eras.label: Era Thirteen · Proverbs 16-17
eras.name: The LORD's Sovereignty Over Plans, and the Conduct of Kings
eras.dates: Chapter 16 opens with some of the book's clearest statements that human intention is real but the LORD's purposes still prevail over it, before both chapters turn to the conduct expected of kings and the value of a well-tested, faithful friend.

events.title: Chapter 16: "A Person Plans His Course, but the LORD Directs His Steps"
events.detail: A chapter built almost entirely around divine sovereignty over human intention: a person's plans belong to them, but the outcome belongs to God, closing with the striking claim that even something as arbitrary as "the dice thrown into the lap" has its decision "from the LORD."

verses.text: A person plans his course, but the LORD [Yahweh] directs his steps.
The dice are thrown into the lap, but their every decision is from the LORD [Yahweh].

events.title: Chapter 17: The Crucible Tests Silver, the LORD Tests Hearts
events.detail: A chapter weighted toward relationships under pressure: a friend who "loves at all times," the cost of repaying evil for good, and the recurring image of the crucible and furnace as a picture of how the LORD tests the human heart.

verses.text: The crucible is for refining silver and the furnace is for gold; likewise the LORD [Yahweh] tests hearts.
A friend loves at all times, and a relative is born to help in adversity.

eras.label: Era Fourteen · Proverbs 18-19
eras.name: Words, Wealth, and Friendship
eras.dates: Two chapters returning to the tongue's power over life and death, the danger of isolating oneself from community, and the LORD's own involvement in ordinary domestic matters, including the striking claim that a prudent wife is his gift rather than mere inheritance.

events.title: Chapter 18: "Death and Life Are in the Power of the Tongue"
events.detail: One of the book's most quoted single lines states the tongue's power in the starkest possible terms, framed by warnings against isolating oneself from community and rushing to give an answer before actually listening.

verses.text: Death and life are in the power of the tongue, and those who love its use will eat its fruit.
There are companions who harm one another, but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother.

events.title: Chapter 19: A Prudent Wife Is From the LORD
events.detail: The chapter weighs poverty, integrity, and family loyalty, including the claim that while a house and wealth are inherited from parents, "a prudent wife is from the LORD": a gift attributed directly to God rather than to family fortune.

verses.text: A house and wealth are inherited from parents, but a prudent wife is from the LORD [Yahweh].
The one who is gracious to the poor lends to the LORD [Yahweh], and the LORD [Yahweh] will repay him for his good deed.

eras.label: Era Fifteen · Proverbs 20-21
eras.name: Kings, Justice, and the Sluggard
eras.dates: The conduct expected of kings continues to run through both chapters, alongside a return to the sluggard who will not plow in season, and one of the book's clearest statements that even a king's heart is entirely in the LORD's hand.

events.title: Chapter 20: "Diverse Weights the LORD Abhors"
events.detail: Honest business practice returns as a theme, dishonest weights and measures are twice called an abomination to the LORD, alongside a warning against the sluggard who will not plow in the planting season and so has nothing at harvest.

verses.text: Diverse weights and diverse measures— the LORD [Yahweh] abhors both of them.
The sluggard will not plow during the planting season, so at harvest time he asks for grain but has nothing.

events.title: Chapter 21: "The King's Heart Is in the Hand of the LORD"
events.detail: The chapter opens with one of the book's boldest claims about divine sovereignty, that even a king's heart is directed by the LORD "like channels of water", before closing with the recognition that ultimate victory, even in battle, comes from him alone.

verses.text: The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD [Yahweh] like channels of water; he turns it wherever he wants.
A horse is prepared for the day of battle, but the victory is from the LORD [Yahweh].

eras.label: Era Sixteen · Proverbs 22:1-16
eras.name: The Close of Solomon's First Collection
eras.dates: The proverbs attributed directly to Solomon close on a note of practical ethics (a good name is worth more than wealth, and the rich and the poor share the same Maker) including the single most famous verse in the book about raising children.

events.title: "Train a Child in the Way He Should Go"
events.detail: Solomon's opening collection closes with sixteen final sayings, including the book's best-known line about child-rearing and the reminder that "the rich and the poor are met together; the LORD is the Creator of them both."

verses.text: Train a child in the way that he should go, and when he is old he will not turn from it.
The rich and the poor are met together; the LORD [Yahweh] is the Creator of them both.

eras.label: Era Seventeen · Proverbs 22:17-24:22
eras.name: "The Words of the Wise" — Thirty Sayings
eras.dates: A new, explicitly named collection begins at 22:17, "the words of the wise", shifting from one-line antithetic sayings to short paragraph-length exhortations addressed directly to "my son," covering table manners with the powerful, the danger of wine, and a fresh warning against envying the wicked.

events.title: "Incline Your Ear": the Thirty Sayings Begin
events.detail: The new collection announces itself as thirty specific sayings meant to give "true and reliable words," opening with instructions not to exploit the poor or move an ancient boundary stone set by one's ancestors.

verses.text: Do not move an ancient boundary stone that was put in place by your ancestors.

events.title: The Ruler's Table, and a Warning Against Wine
events.detail: A vivid extended warning against wine closes the chapter, "your eyes will see strange things" and it "bites like a snake", framed by instructions on restraint at a ruler's table and honoring aging parents.

verses.text: Do not look on the wine when it is red, when it sparkles in the cup, when it goes down smoothly. Afterward it bites like a snake and stings like a viper.

events.title: Do Not Envy Evil People
events.detail: The collection warns against envying wicked people whose hearts "contemplate violence," and delivers one of the book's sharpest lines on moral responsibility, that claiming ignorance does not excuse inaction when others are being led to death.

verses.text: Deliver those being taken away to death, and hold back those slipping to the slaughter. If you say, "But we did not know about this," won't the one who evaluates hearts discern it?

eras.label: Era Eighteen · Proverbs 24:23-34
eras.name: "These Also Are From the Wise", and the Sluggard's Field
eras.dates: A short additional collection on impartial justice closes with Solomon's own eyewitness account of walking past a sluggard's overgrown, wall-broken vineyard: the closest thing in the book to a personal field observation turned into a lesson.

events.title: Impartial Justice
events.detail: A brief addendum reinforces impartiality in judgment and honesty as a witness, condemning both those who declare the guilty innocent and those who deceive with false testimony.

events.title: Solomon Passes a Sluggard's Ruined Field
events.detail: In an unusually personal aside, Solomon describes walking past the overgrown, weed-choked vineyard of "one who lacks sense," drawing the lesson in his own voice after "scrutinizing it" and "taking in a lesson" firsthand.

verses.text: I passed by the field of a sluggard, by the vineyard of one who lacks sense. I saw that thorns had grown up all over it… Then I scrutinized it. I was putting my mind to it— I saw; I took in a lesson.

eras.label: Era Nineteen · Proverbs 25-27
eras.name: Hezekiah's Collection: Proverbs of Comparison
eras.dates: A new heading at 25:1 marks proverbs "copied" by King Hezekiah's men generations after Solomon, and this collection leans heavily on the simile form ("like apples of gold," "like a muddied spring") culminating in the sharpened-iron picture of real friendship.

events.title: Chapter 25: Kings, Silver Refined, and Apples of Gold
events.detail: The chapter opens by naming its source, men of King Hezekiah copied these, and moves through images of refining silver from dross and "a word skillfully spoken" being like apples of gold in silver settings, closing with self-control as a city's own defensive wall.

verses.text: Like apples of gold in settings of silver, so is a word skillfully spoken.
These also are proverbs of Solomon, which the men of King Hezekiah of Judah copied.

events.title: Chapter 26: A Chapter Given Almost Entirely to Fools
events.detail: An unusually unified chapter devoted almost entirely to the fool, including the famously paired instructions to both "not answer a fool according to his folly" and, immediately after, to "answer a fool according to his folly," each for its own distinct reason.

verses.text: Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you yourself also be like him. Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own opinion.

events.title: Chapter 27: "As Iron Sharpens Iron"
events.detail: One of the book's most enduring images of friendship appears here, iron sharpening iron, alongside practical instruction to know the condition of one's own flocks and herds, since wealth and status do not last from one generation to the next automatically.

verses.text: As iron sharpens iron, so a person sharpens his friend.
Do not boast about tomorrow; for you do not know what a day may bring forth.

eras.label: Era Twenty · Proverbs 28-29
eras.name: Hezekiah's Collection: Rulers, the Righteous, and the Wicked
eras.dates: The Hezekiah collection closes with two chapters weighted toward governance: how rulers rise and fall by justice or oppression, and the recurring principle that a nation's condition tracks the moral condition of who holds power within it.

events.title: Chapter 28: The Wicked Flee Without Pursuit
events.detail: The chapter opens with the striking image of the wicked fleeing though no one chases them, while the righteous are as confident as a lion, and repeatedly ties a nation's stability to whether its rulers are discerning or oppressive.

verses.text: The wicked person fled, though no one was pursuing, but the righteous person can be as confident as a lion.
The one who covers his transgressions will not prosper, but whoever confesses them and forsakes them will find mercy.

events.title: Chapter 29: When the Righteous Rule, the People Rejoice
events.detail: The final chapter of this collection returns repeatedly to the effect of leadership on an entire population (when the righteous increase the people rejoice, but when the wicked rule they groan) closing the collection on trust in the LORD as the true source of justice.

verses.text: When the righteous become numerous, the people rejoice; when the wicked rule, the people groan.
The fear of people becomes a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD [Yahweh] will be set on high.

eras.label: Era Twenty-One · Proverbs 30
eras.name: The Words of Agur: Riddles and Numerical Sayings
eras.dates: An otherwise unknown figure named Agur opens with an unusual confession of his own ignorance before God, then shifts into the book's most distinctive literary form: a run of "three things… four things" numerical riddles built from observations of the natural world.

events.title: Agur's Confession and Prayer
events.detail: Agur opens by confessing he lacks even basic human understanding, let alone "knowledge of the Holy One," then offers the book's only direct prayer, asking not for poverty or riches, but only his "allotted portion of bread," for fear that too much would make him deny the LORD and too little would make him steal.

verses.text: do not give me poverty or riches; feed me with my allotted portion of bread, lest I become satisfied and act deceptively and say, "Who is the LORD [Yahweh]?" Or lest I become poor and steal and demean the name of my God [Elohim].

events.title: "Three Things… Four Things": Numerical Riddles
events.detail: Agur turns to the book's most distinctive form, a series of "three things, even four" riddles drawn from nature: the way of an eagle in the sky, ants storing food despite little strength, and a lizard that nonetheless finds its way into royal palaces.

verses.text: There are four things on earth that are small, but they are exceedingly wise: Ants are creatures with little strength, but they prepare their food in the summer.

eras.label: Era Twenty-Two · Proverbs 31
eras.name: The Words of King Lemuel, and the Wife of Noble Character
eras.dates: An unknown king named Lemuel first passes on his mother's warning against wine and the neglect of justice, and the book closes with its most famous single unit: a twenty-two-line acrostic poem praising a capable, hard-working, God-fearing wife, each line beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet.

events.title: Lemuel's Mother's Instruction to the King
events.detail: King Lemuel recalls his mother's warning that kings must not let wine distract them from their duty, and that a ruler's mouth exists above all to "plead the cause of the poor and needy."

verses.text: Open your mouth on behalf of those unable to speak, for the legal rights of all the dying. Open your mouth, judge in righteousness, and plead the cause of the poor and needy.

events.title: The Wife of Noble Character
events.detail: The book's closing poem is a twenty-two-line acrostic, each line beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, praising a wife of tireless, competent, generous labor, resolving the book's earlier warnings against the adulterous woman into a single sustained portrait of the woman actually worth finding, whose worth is "far more than rubies" and whose defining trait is not beauty but that she "fears the LORD."

verses.text: Who can find a wife of noble character? For her value is far more than rubies.
Charm is deceitful and beauty is fleeting. A woman who fears the LORD [Yahweh]—she makes herself praiseworthy.
